questions.question: Prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram if its diagonals bisect each other.
questions.explanation: Given: Quadrilateral ABCD whose diagonals AC and BD bisect each other at O. To prove: ABCD is a parallelogram. Proof: In ΔAOB ↔ ΔCOD: AO ≅ OC, BO ≅ OD and ∠AOB ≅ ∠COD (vertically opposite). So ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD (S.A.S.), giving ∠OAB ≅ ∠OCD ⇒ AB ∥ CD. Similarly ΔAOD ≅ ΔCOB gives AD ∥ BC. Hence ABCD is a parallelogram. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that if both pairs of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are congruent, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
questions.explanation: Given: Quadrilateral ABCD with AB ≅ CD and AD ≅ BC. To prove: ABCD is a parallelogram. Proof: Draw the diagonal BD. In ΔABD ↔ ΔCDB: AB ≅ CD (given), AD ≅ CB (given), BD ≅ BD (common). So ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB (S.S.S.), giving ∠ABD ≅ ∠CDB and ∠ADB ≅ ∠CBD. These are pairs of alternate angles, so AB ∥ CD and AD ∥ BC. Hence ABCD is a parallelogram. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that if a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, its diagonals form two congruent triangles.
questions.answer: Each diagonal divides the parallelogram into two congruent triangles.
questions.explanation: Given: ABCD is a parallelogram with diagonal AC. To prove: ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA. Proof: AB ≅ CD and BC ≅ DA (opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent), and AC ≅ AC (common). Hence ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA by S.S.S. Similarly, diagonal BD gives ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that if the angles formed with every side of a quadrilateral are supplementary, then it is a parallelogram.
questions.explanation: Given: Quadrilateral ABCD in which the interior angles on each side are supplementary, e.g. ∠A + ∠B = 180° and ∠B + ∠C = 180°. To prove: ABCD is a parallelogram. Proof: ∠A + ∠B = 180° means the interior angles on the same side of the line AB are supplementary, so AD ∥ BC. Similarly ∠B + ∠C = 180° gives AB ∥ CD. Hence ABCD is a parallelogram. Q.E.D.

questions.question: If the line segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and its length is 4 cm, what is the length of the third side?
questions.explanation: The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is equal to half the third side. So 4 = ½(third side) ⇒ third side = 8 cm.

questions.question: Prove that the line segments joining the mid-points of the opposite sides of a quadrilateral bisect each other.
questions.answer: The two joining segments bisect each other.
questions.explanation: Given: Quadrilateral ABCD with P, Q, R, S the mid-points of AB, BC, CD, DA. To prove: the segments PR and QS bisect each other. Proof: In ΔABC, PQ joins the mid-points of AB and BC, so PQ ∥ AC and PQ = ½AC. In ΔADC, SR joins the mid-points of AD and DC, so SR ∥ AC and SR = ½AC. Thus PQ ∥ SR and PQ ≅ SR, so PQRS is a parallelogram. The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, hence PR and QS bisect each other. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that the line segments joining the mid-points of the sides of a quadrilateral, taken in order, form a parallelogram.
questions.explanation: Given: Quadrilateral ABCD with P, Q, R, S the mid-points of AB, BC, CD, DA. To prove: PQRS is a parallelogram. Proof: In ΔABC, PQ joins mid-points so PQ ∥ AC and PQ = ½AC. In ΔADC, SR joins mid-points so SR ∥ AC and SR = ½AC. Hence PQ ∥ SR and PQ ≅ SR, so one pair of opposite sides of PQRS are equal and parallel; therefore PQRS is a parallelogram. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that the line segment passing through the mid-point of one side and parallel to another side of a triangle also bisects the third side.
questions.answer: The line bisects the third side.
questions.explanation: Given: ΔABC with M the mid-point of AB; through M a line is drawn parallel to BC meeting AC at N. To prove: N is the mid-point of AC. Proof: The segment joining the mid-points of AB and AC is parallel to BC. Through M there is only one line parallel to BC, so this segment must be MN. Hence N is the mid-point of AC, i.e. the line bisects AC. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that the four triangles obtained by joining the mid-points of the three sides of a triangle are all congruent to each other.
questions.answer: All four small triangles are congruent.
questions.explanation: Given: ΔABC with D, E, F the mid-points of BC, CA, AB. To prove: ΔAFE ≅ ΔFBD ≅ ΔEDC ≅ ΔDEF. Proof: By the mid-point theorem, EF = ½BC = BD = DC, FD = ½AC = AE = EC and DE = ½AB = AF = FB. Each of the four triangles therefore has sides ½AB, ½BC, ½CA. Hence all four triangles are congruent by S.S.S. Q.E.D.

questions.question: If the three medians of a triangle are congruent, prove that the triangle is equilateral.
questions.explanation: Given: ΔABC with medians of lengths m<sub>a</sub>, m<sub>b</sub>, m<sub>c</sub> such that m<sub>a</sub> = m<sub>b</sub> = m<sub>c</sub>. Proof: Using m<sub>a</sub> = ½√(2b<sup>2</sup> + 2c<sup>2</sup> − a<sup>2</sup>), the equality m<sub>a</sub> = m<sub>b</sub> gives 2b<sup>2</sup> + 2c<sup>2</sup> − a<sup>2</sup> = 2c<sup>2</sup> + 2a<sup>2</sup> − b<sup>2</sup> ⇒ 3b<sup>2</sup> = 3a<sup>2</sup> ⇒ a = b. Similarly m<sub>b</sub> = m<sub>c</sub> gives b = c. Hence a = b = c and the triangle is equilateral. Q.E.D.

questions.question: The medians PB, QC and RA of ΔPQR meet at point G. Show that G is the centroid of ΔPQR.
questions.explanation: Since PB, QC and RA are the three medians of ΔPQR and they are concurrent at G, and by definition the point of concurrency of the medians of a triangle is its centroid, G is the centroid of ΔPQR. Moreover, by Theorem 10.1.4 the centroid G is the point of trisection of each median, so PG : GB = QG : GC = RG : GA = 2 : 1. Q.E.D.

questions.question: In the given figure, the length of GR is 2 cm; find the length of AG.
questions.explanation: G is the centroid, so it divides the median RA in the ratio RG : GA = 2 : 1. Given GR = 2 cm, we get GA = ½ × 2 = 1 cm. Hence AG = 1 cm.

questions.question: The triangle formed by joining the mid-points of the sides of a triangle is similar to (equivalent in shape to) the original triangle.
questions.answer: The medial triangle is similar to the original triangle (each side is half, area one-fourth).
questions.explanation: Given: ΔABC with D, E, F the mid-points of BC, CA, AB. To prove: ΔDEF is similar to ΔABC. Proof: By the mid-point theorem, DE ∥ AB, EF ∥ BC and FD ∥ CA. Hence the corresponding angles are equal (e.g. ∠DEF = ∠B, ∠DFE = ∠A), so ΔDEF ~ ΔABC. Also each side of ΔDEF is half the corresponding side of ΔABC, so the area of ΔDEF is one-fourth the area of ΔABC. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that the line segment joining the mid-points of the non-parallel sides of a trapezium is parallel to the parallel sides and is equal to half their sum.
questions.answer: The median of the trapezium = ½(sum of parallel sides) and is parallel to them.
questions.explanation: Given: Trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC; M, N are the mid-points of the non-parallel sides AD, BC. To prove: MN ∥ AB ∥ DC and MN = ½(AB + DC). Proof: Draw diagonal AC, meeting MN at P. In ΔADC, M is the mid-point of AD and MP ∥ DC, so P is the mid-point of AC and MP = ½DC. In ΔABC, P is the mid-point of AC and N is the mid-point of BC, so PN ∥ AB and PN = ½AB. Thus M, P, N are collinear, MN ∥ AB ∥ DC, and MN = MP + PN = ½DC + ½AB = ½(AB + DC). Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that every line segment drawn from the vertex to the base of a triangle is bisected by the line joining the mid-points of the other two sides.
questions.answer: The mid-segment bisects any cevian from the vertex to the base.
questions.explanation: Given: ΔABC with M, N the mid-points of AB, AC; a segment from A meets BC at D and meets MN at E. To prove: AE ≅ ED (MN bisects AD). Proof: MN joins the mid-points of AB and AC, so MN ∥ BC, hence ME ∥ BD. In ΔABD, M is the mid-point of AB and ME ∥ BD, so by the converse of the mid-point theorem E is the mid-point of AD. Hence AE ≅ ED. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are ________.
questions.explanation: The opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal in length (congruent).

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are ________.
questions.explanation: The opposite (and corresponding) angles of a parallelogram are equal in measure.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In a triangle, medians are ________.
questions.explanation: The three medians of a triangle are concurrent (they meet at a single point, the centroid).

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In a parallelogram, the diagonals ________ each other.
questions.explanation: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In a parallelogram, corresponding angles are ________.
questions.explanation: Corresponding (and opposite) angles of a parallelogram are equal in measure.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The sum of the measures of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is equal to ________.
questions.explanation: A quadrilateral can be split into two triangles, so the sum of its interior angles is 2 × 180° = 360°.

questions.question: The diagonals of a square are ________ to each other.
questions.explanation: The diagonals of a square are equal (congruent) and they bisect each other at right angles (perpendicular). Hence both (a) and (c) are correct.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Perpendicular  b) Non congruent  c) Congruent  d) Both 'a' and 'c'

questions.question: The sum of the measures of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is:
questions.explanation: The sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is 360° = 4 right angles.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 2 right angles  b) 4 right angles  c) 3 right angles  d) none of these

questions.question: The measure of the line segment joining the mid-points of AB and AC of ΔABC is 3.5 cm, then m BC =
questions.explanation: The mid-segment equals half the third side: 3.5 = ½(BC) ⇒ BC = 7 cm.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 4.5 cm  b) 5.5 cm  c) 6 cm  d) 7 cm

questions.question: Two medians AD and BE of ΔABC intersect each other at G. If m GD = 1.7 cm, then m AG =
questions.explanation: The centroid G divides a median in the ratio 2 : 1, so AG = 2 × GD = 2 × 1.7 = 3.4 cm.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 2.7 cm  b) 8.85 cm  c) 3.4 cm  d) 5.1 cm

questions.question: If the sum of the measures of ∠A and ∠C of a parallelogram ABCD is 130°, then m∠B =
questions.explanation: In a parallelogram ∠A ≅ ∠C, so each = 65°. Consecutive angles are supplementary: ∠B = 180° − 65° = 115°.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 25°  b) 115°  c) 65°  d) none of these

questions.question: If the opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal in measure and none of them is a right angle, then the quadrilateral is a:
questions.explanation: A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite angles equal is a parallelogram. Since none of the angles is a right angle, it is not a rectangle or square, so it is a (non-rectangular) parallelogram.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Square  b) Parallelogram  c) Trapezium  d) Rectangle

questions.question: Centroid is the common point of intersection of:
questions.explanation: The centroid is the point of concurrency of the three medians of a triangle.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Medians of a triangle  b) Diagonals of a parallelogram  c) Angle bisectors of a triangle  d) Perpendicular bisectors of a triangle

questions.question: A point on a median of a triangle is:
questions.explanation: None of the listed properties holds for an arbitrary point on a median. (The circumcentre, not a general median point, is equidistant from the vertices, and it need not lie on a median.) Hence the correct option is (d) none of these.

options.text: equidistant from the mid-points of its sides

questions.optionsRaw: a) equidistant from its vertices  b) equidistant from the mid-points of its sides  c) equidistant from its altitudes  d) none of these

questions.question: Prove that the point of intersection of the right bisectors of any two sides of a triangle is equidistant from all the vertices of the triangle.
questions.answer: The point is equidistant from all three vertices.
questions.explanation: Given: ΔABC with the right bisectors of AB and AC meeting at O. To prove: OA ≅ OB ≅ OC. Proof: O lies on the right bisector of AB, so OA ≅ OB. O also lies on the right bisector of AC, so OA ≅ OC. Hence OA ≅ OB ≅ OC, i.e. O is equidistant from the three vertices. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that the centre of a circle is on the right bisectors of each of its chords.
questions.answer: The centre lies on the right bisector of every chord.
questions.explanation: Given: A circle with centre O and a chord AB. To prove: O lies on the right bisector of AB. Proof: OA ≅ OB (radii of the same circle). A point equidistant from the two ends of a line segment lies on the right bisector of that segment. Hence O lies on the right bisector of AB. As AB is an arbitrary chord, the result holds for every chord. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Where will be the centre of a circle passing through three non-collinear points, and why?
questions.answer: At the point of intersection of the right bisectors of the segments joining the points.
questions.explanation: Let A, B, C be three non-collinear points. Draw the right bisectors of AB and BC; let them meet at O. Since O lies on the right bisector of AB, OA ≅ OB; since O lies on the right bisector of BC, OB ≅ OC. Hence OA ≅ OB ≅ OC, so O is equidistant from A, B and C. Therefore a circle with centre O and radius OA passes through all three points, i.e. the centre is the point of intersection of the right bisectors of the segments joining the points.

questions.question: If two circles intersect each other at points A and B, prove that the line passing through their centres will be the right bisector of AB.
questions.answer: The line of centres is the right bisector of the common chord AB.
questions.explanation: Given: Two circles with centres O and O′ intersecting at A and B. To prove: OO′ is the right bisector of AB. Proof: OA ≅ OB (radii of the same circle) and O′A ≅ O′B (radii of the same circle). Thus each of O and O′ is equidistant from A and B, so each lies on the right bisector of AB. Since two points determine a line, the line OO′ is the right bisector of AB. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Three markets A, B and C are not on the same line. The business men of these markets want to construct a Masjid at a place equidistant from these markets. Prove that this place is equidistant from all three markets.
questions.answer: The Masjid is at the circumcentre of ΔABC (intersection of right bisectors of AB, BC, CA).
questions.explanation: The required point must be equidistant from A, B and C. Join A, B and C to form ΔABC. Draw the right bisectors of AB and AC; let them meet at O. Since O is on the right bisector of AB, OA ≅ OB; since O is on the right bisector of AC, OA ≅ OC. Hence OA ≅ OB ≅ OC. Therefore the Masjid built at O is equidistant from all three markets. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that in an acute triangle the circumcentre falls in the interior of the triangle.
questions.answer: The circumcentre lies inside an acute triangle.
questions.explanation: Let O be the circumcentre of ΔABC. Then ∠BOC = 2∠A, ∠COA = 2∠B and ∠AOB = 2∠C (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference). Since ΔABC is acute, ∠A, ∠B, ∠C are each less than 90°, so each central angle (∠BOC, ∠COA, ∠AOB) is less than 180°. When all three central angles are less than 180°, the centre O lies strictly inside the triangle. Hence in an acute triangle the circumcentre falls in the interior. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that the right bisectors of the four sides of an isosceles trapezium are concurrent.
questions.answer: All four right bisectors pass through one point.
questions.explanation: Given: An isosceles trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC and AD ≅ BC. To prove: the right bisectors of AB, BC, CD, DA are concurrent. Proof: Every isosceles trapezium is cyclic; let O be the centre of its circumcircle. Then OA ≅ OB ≅ OC ≅ OD (radii). Since O is equidistant from the endpoints of each side, O lies on the right bisector of each of the four sides. Hence all four right bisectors pass through O, i.e. they are concurrent. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.
questions.answer: The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent (at the orthocentre).
questions.explanation: Given: ΔABC with altitudes AD ⊥ BC, BE ⊥ CA, CF ⊥ AB. To prove: AD, BE and CF are concurrent. Proof: Through A draw a line parallel to BC, through B a line parallel to CA and through C a line parallel to AB; these lines form a larger triangle A′B′C′ in which A, B, C are the mid-points of the sides B′C′, C′A′, A′B′ respectively. Since AD ⊥ BC and BC ∥ B′C′, we get AD ⊥ B′C′; and A is the mid-point of B′C′. Hence AD is the right bisector of B′C′. Similarly BE and CF are the right bisectors of C′A′ and A′B′. The right bisectors of a triangle are concurrent, so AD, BE and CF are concurrent. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Two isosceles triangles have a common base; prove that the line joining the vertices bisects the common base at right angle.
questions.answer: The line joining the vertices is the right bisector of the common base.
questions.explanation: Given: Isosceles ΔABC and ΔDBC on the same base BC, with AB ≅ AC and DB ≅ DC. To prove: AD bisects BC at right angles. Proof: In ΔABC, AB ≅ AC, so A is equidistant from B and C and lies on the right bisector of BC. In ΔDBC, DB ≅ DC, so D also lies on the right bisector of BC. Hence the line AD is the right bisector of BC, i.e. it bisects BC at right angles. Q.E.D.

questions.question: If the bisector of an angle of a triangle bisects the opposite side, prove that the triangle is isosceles.
questions.explanation: Given: In ΔABC, AD bisects ∠A and BD ≅ DC. To prove: AB ≅ AC. Proof: Produce AD to E such that AD ≅ DE, and join C to E. In ΔADB ↔ ΔEDC: AD ≅ DE (construction), BD ≅ DC (given) and ∠ADB ≅ ∠EDC (vertically opposite). So ΔADB ≅ ΔEDC (S.A.S.), giving ∠BAD ≅ ∠CED and AB ≅ EC. But ∠BAD ≅ ∠DAC (AD bisects ∠A), so ∠CED ≅ ∠DAC, i.e. ∠CEA ≅ ∠CAE, whence AC ≅ CE. Hence AB ≅ EC ≅ AC, so AB ≅ AC. Q.E.D.

questions.question: In an isosceles ΔABC, m AB = m AC. Prove that the perpendiculars from the vertices B and C to their opposite sides are equal.
questions.explanation: Given: ΔABC with AB ≅ AC; BE ⊥ AC and CF ⊥ AB. To prove: BE ≅ CF. Proof: In ΔBEC ↔ ΔCFB: ∠BEC ≅ ∠CFB (= 90°); BC ≅ BC (common); and ∠EBC ≅ ∠FCB (each equals 90° − a base angle, and the base angles are equal). Hence ΔBEC ≅ ΔCFB (A.A.S.), so BE ≅ CF. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that, if two altitudes of a triangle are congruent, the triangle is an isosceles.
questions.explanation: Given: ΔABC with altitudes BE ⊥ AC and CF ⊥ AB such that BE ≅ CF. To prove: ΔABC is isosceles. Proof: The area of ΔABC is ½(AC)(BE) = ½(AB)(CF). Since BE ≅ CF, we get AC ≅ AB. Hence the triangle is isosceles. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that a point in the interior of a triangle equidistant from all three sides lies on the bisector of all the three angles of the triangle.
questions.answer: The point lies on the bisectors of all three angles.
questions.explanation: Given: A point P inside ΔABC that is equidistant from the three sides AB, BC and CA. To prove: P lies on the bisectors of ∠A, ∠B and ∠C. Proof: Since P is equidistant from the arms AB and AC of ∠A, by the converse of the angle-bisector theorem P lies on the bisector of ∠A. Similarly, being equidistant from the arms of ∠B, P lies on the bisector of ∠B; and being equidistant from the arms of ∠C, P lies on the bisector of ∠C. Hence P lies on the bisectors of all three angles. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Write 'T' for True or 'F' for False: Bisection of a side means we divide the given side into two equal parts.
questions.explanation: To bisect a side means to divide it into two equal parts.

questions.question: Write 'T' for True or 'F' for False: In a right-angled isosceles triangle each angle on the base is 45°.
questions.explanation: A right-angled isosceles triangle has one angle 90° and two equal base angles; each base angle = (180° − 90°)/2 = 45°.

questions.question: Write 'T' for True or 'F' for False: A triangle of congruent sides has congruent angles.
questions.explanation: If the sides of a triangle are congruent (equal), the angles opposite them are also congruent (equal).

questions.question: There are ________ acute angles in an acute-angled triangle.
questions.explanation: In an acute-angled triangle all three angles are acute, so there are three acute angles.
questions.optionsRaw: a) One  b) Two  c) Three  d) None

questions.question: A point equidistant from the end points of a line segment is on the ________ of it.
questions.explanation: The set of all points equidistant from the ends of a segment is its right (perpendicular) bisector.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Right bisector  b) Perpendicular  c) Centre  d) Mid-point

questions.question: ________ of the sides of an acute-angled triangle intersect each other inside the triangle.
questions.explanation: The right bisectors of the sides of an acute triangle meet (intersect) at a point inside the triangle (its circumcentre).
questions.optionsRaw: a) Perpendicular  b) The right bisector  c) Obtuse  d) Acute

questions.question: The bisectors of the angles of a triangle are ________.
questions.explanation: The bisectors of the three angles of a triangle are concurrent (they meet at the incentre).
questions.optionsRaw: a) Concurrent  b) Collinear  c) Do not intersect  d) Unequal

chapters.title: Sides and Angles of a Triangle

questions.question: O is an interior point of the ΔABC. Show that m OA + m OB + m OC > ½(m AB + m BC + m CA).
questions.explanation: Proof: By the triangle inequality: in ΔAOB, OA + OB > AB; in ΔBOC, OB + OC > BC; in ΔCOA, OC + OA > CA. Adding these three inequalities gives 2(OA + OB + OC) > AB + BC + CA, hence OA + OB + OC > ½(AB + BC + CA). Q.E.D.

questions.question: In ΔABC, m∠B = 70° and m∠C = 45°. Which of the sides of the triangle is the longest?
questions.explanation: The third angle is ∠A = 180° − (70° + 45°) = 65°. The greatest angle is ∠B = 70°, and the side opposite the greatest angle is the longest. The side opposite ∠B is AC. Hence AC is the longest side.

questions.question: In ΔABC, m∠A = 55° and m∠B = 65°. Which of the sides of the triangle is the smallest?
questions.explanation: The third angle is ∠C = 180° − (55° + 65°) = 60°. The smallest angle is ∠A = 55°, and the side opposite the smallest angle is the smallest. The side opposite ∠A is BC. Hence BC is the smallest side.

questions.question: True or False: The sum of the two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side.
questions.explanation: This is the triangle inequality: the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side.

questions.question: True or False: The difference of two sides of a triangle is larger than the third side.
questions.explanation: The difference of any two sides of a triangle is always less than the third side (from the triangle inequality), so the statement is false.

questions.question: True or False: The perpendicular distance from a point to a line is the longest distance between them.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular from a point to a line is the shortest (not longest) distance from the point to the line.

questions.question: True or False: In a right-angled triangle the largest angle is of 100°.
questions.explanation: In a right-angled triangle the largest angle is the right angle, 90°, not 100°.

questions.question: True or False: A perpendicular on a line always makes an angle of 90°.
questions.explanation: By definition a perpendicular to a line meets it at 90°.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In any right-angled triangle, ________ is the longest side of the triangle.
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) is the longest side of a right-angled triangle.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In a right-angled triangle, the sum of the measures of the sides containing the right angle is ________ than the measure of the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation: The two legs add up to more than the hypotenuse (triangle inequality), so the sum is greater.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In ΔABC, m∠A = 50° and m∠B = 30°. Side ________ will be longer than its other sides.
questions.explanation: The third angle is ∠C = 180° − (50° + 30°) = 100°, the greatest angle. The side opposite the greatest angle is the longest, and AB is opposite ∠C. Hence side AB is the longest.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The length of a diagonal of any quadrilateral is ________ than the sum of the measures of its two adjacent sides.
questions.explanation: Considering the triangle formed by the diagonal and two adjacent sides, the diagonal is less than the sum of the other two sides (triangle inequality).

questions.question: The measure of one side of an equilateral triangle is 6 cm; then the length of its median is ________ 9 cm.
questions.explanation: The median of an equilateral triangle of side a is (√3/2)a = (√3/2)×6 = 3√3 ≈ 5.2 cm, which is less than 9 cm.
questions.optionsRaw: a) less than  b) greater than  c) equal to  d) none of the above

questions.question: The perimeter of a rectangle is 22 cm; then the length of its diagonal is ________ 11 cm.
questions.explanation: Perimeter 22 cm means the sum of two adjacent sides is 11 cm. The diagonal is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the two adjacent sides, so it is less than their sum, i.e. less than 11 cm.
questions.optionsRaw: a) equal to  b) greater than  c) less than  d) none of the above

questions.question: Construct ΔPQR such that m PQ = m QR = 4.6 cm and m∠Q = 35°.
questions.answer: Construction of an isosceles triangle with equal sides 4.6 cm and included angle 35°.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw QR = 4.6 cm. (ii) At Q construct ∠RQX = 35°. (iii) With Q as centre and radius 4.6 cm, mark P on QX. (iv) Join P to R. ΔPQR is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔABC such that m AB = m AC = 5.1 cm and m∠A = 65°.
questions.answer: Construction of an isosceles triangle with equal sides 5.1 cm and included angle 65°.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw AB = 5.1 cm. (ii) At A construct ∠BAX = 65°. (iii) With A as centre and radius 5.1 cm, mark C on AX. (iv) Join B to C. ΔABC is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔLMN such that m LM = 3.7 cm, m MN = 2.5 cm and ∠M = 50°.
questions.answer: Construction of a triangle with two sides and the included angle (S.A.S.).
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw LM = 3.7 cm. (ii) At M construct ∠LMX = 50°. (iii) With M as centre and radius 2.5 cm, mark N on MX. (iv) Join L to N. ΔLMN is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔABC such that m AB = 3.5 cm, m BC = 2.7 cm and ∠B = 110°.
questions.answer: Construction of a triangle with two sides and the included angle (S.A.S.).
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw AB = 3.5 cm. (ii) At B construct ∠ABX = 110°. (iii) With B as centre and radius 2.7 cm, mark C on BX. (iv) Join A to C. ΔABC is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔXYZ such that m XY = 4.1 cm, m YZ = 5 cm and ∠Z = 80°.
questions.answer: Construction of a triangle with two sides and an angle opposite one of them.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw YZ = 5 cm. (ii) At Z construct ∠YZX = 80°. (iii) With Y as centre and radius 4.1 cm, draw an arc cutting ZX at X. (iv) Join X to Y. ΔXYZ is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔDEF given m DE = 5 cm, m∠D = 45° and m∠E = 60°.
questions.answer: Construction of a triangle with one side and two angles (A.S.A.).
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw DE = 5 cm. (ii) At D construct ∠XDE = 45°. (iii) At E construct ∠YED = 60°. (iv) Let DX and EY meet at F. ΔDEF is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔLMN given m LM = 6 cm, m∠L = 75° and m∠M = 45°.
questions.answer: Construction of a triangle with one side and two angles (A.S.A.).
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw LM = 6 cm. (ii) At L construct ∠XLM = 75°. (iii) At M construct ∠YML = 45°. (iv) Let LX and MY meet at N. ΔLMN is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔABC given m BC = 5.8 cm, m∠A = 30° and m∠B = 45°.
questions.answer: Construction of a triangle (A.S.A. after finding ∠C = 105°).
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) ∠C = 180° − (30° + 45°) = 105°. (ii) Draw BC = 5.8 cm. (iii) At B construct ∠B = 45°. (iv) At C construct ∠C = 105°. (v) The two rays meet at A. ΔABC is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔABC when m AC = 4.5 cm, m BC = 4.1 cm and m∠B = 75°.
questions.answer: Construction of a triangle with two sides and an angle opposite one of them.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw BC = 4.1 cm. (ii) At B construct ∠CBX = 75°. (iii) With C as centre and radius 4.5 cm, draw an arc cutting BX at A. (iv) Join A to C. ΔABC is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔABC when m BC = 5 cm, m AB = 5.5 cm and m∠C = 70°.
questions.answer: Construction of a triangle with two sides and an angle opposite one of them.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw BC = 5 cm. (ii) At C construct ∠BCX = 70°. (iii) With B as centre and radius 5.5 cm, draw an arc cutting CX at A. (iv) Join A to B. ΔABC is the required triangle.

questions.question: Construct ΔABC when m AB = 5 cm, m BC = 5.5 cm and m∠A = 45°.
questions.answer: Construction of a triangle with two sides and an angle opposite one of them.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw AB = 5 cm. (ii) At A construct ∠BAX = 45°. (iii) With B as centre and radius 5.5 cm, draw an arc cutting AX at C. (iv) Join B to C. ΔABC is the required triangle.

questions.question: Take a triangle and draw the medians; prove that they are concurrent.
questions.answer: The three medians are concurrent (at the centroid).
questions.explanation: Construction: Draw a triangle ABC; bisect the sides to find their mid-points D, E, F; join each vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side to obtain the medians AD, BE and CF. Conclusion: All three medians pass through a single common point G, so the medians of a triangle are concurrent. That point G is the centroid, and it divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1.

questions.question: Take a triangle and draw the altitudes; prove that they are concurrent.
questions.answer: The three altitudes are concurrent (at the orthocentre).
questions.explanation: Construction: Draw a triangle ABC and construct the perpendicular from each vertex to the opposite side: AD ⊥ BC, BE ⊥ CA, CF ⊥ AB. Conclusion: The three altitudes pass through a single common point O, so the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent. That point O is called the orthocentre.

questions.question: Take a triangle and draw the internal bisectors of the angles; prove that they are concurrent.
questions.answer: The three angle bisectors are concurrent (at the incentre).
questions.explanation: Construction: Draw a triangle ABC and construct the internal bisectors of ∠A, ∠B and ∠C. Conclusion: The three bisectors pass through a single common point I, so the internal bisectors of a triangle are concurrent. That point I is called the incentre, and it is equidistant from the three sides.

questions.question: Construct a triangle ABC in which m BC = 6 cm, m CA = 4 cm and m AB = 5 cm; draw the bisectors of angles A and B.
questions.answer: Construction of ΔABC (sides 6, 4, 5 cm) and its angle bisectors at A and B.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw BC = 6 cm. (ii) With B as centre and radius 5 cm, and with C as centre and radius 4 cm, draw arcs intersecting at A. (iii) Join A to B and A to C. (iv) Construct the bisector of ∠A and the bisector of ∠B; they meet at the incentre I.

questions.question: Construct a triangle PQR in which m PQ = 5.7 cm, m QR = 6.4 cm and m PR = 4.4 cm; draw the altitudes from vertex R and vertex Q.
questions.answer: Construction of ΔPQR (sides 5.7, 6.4, 4.4 cm) and two altitudes.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw QR = 6.4 cm. (ii) With Q as centre and radius 5.7 cm, and with R as centre and radius 4.4 cm, draw arcs intersecting at P. (iii) Join P to Q and P to R. (iv) From R draw RN ⊥ PQ and from Q draw QM ⊥ PR; these are the required altitudes.

questions.question: Construct a triangle STU in which ∠T = 60°, ∠U = 30° and m TU = 7 cm. Find the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of the triangle and prove that they are concurrent.
questions.answer: The perpendicular bisectors are concurrent (at the circumcentre).
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw TU = 7 cm. (ii) At T construct ∠T = 60° and at U construct ∠U = 30°; their rays meet at S. (iii) Construct the perpendicular bisectors of ST, TU and US. Conclusion: All three perpendicular bisectors pass through a common point O, so they are concurrent. O is the circumcentre and is equidistant from S, T and U.

questions.question: Construct a right triangle ABC in which ∠C = 90°, ∠B = 45° and m CB = 5 cm; draw the medians of the triangle.
questions.answer: Construction of the right triangle and its medians.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw CB = 5 cm. (ii) At C construct ∠BCX = 90°. (iii) At B construct ∠CBY = 45°; the rays CX and BY meet at A. (iv) Bisect the three sides to find their mid-points and join each vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side to obtain the three medians, which meet at the centroid G.

questions.question: Construct ΔXYZ, where m YZ = 4.4 cm, m∠Y = 45° and m∠Z = 75°; draw its three medians and show that they are concurrent.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw YZ = 4.4 cm. (ii) At Y construct ∠Y = 45° and at Z construct ∠Z = 75°; the rays meet at X. (iii) Bisect each side and join each vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side to draw the three medians. All three medians pass through a single common point (the centroid), hence they are concurrent.

questions.question: Construct ΔXYZ, where m XY = 4.6 cm, m XZ = 4.6 cm and m∠Y = 60°; draw its three medians and show that they are concurrent.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw XY = 4.6 cm. (ii) At Y construct ∠Y = 60°. (iii) With X as centre and radius 4.6 cm, draw an arc cutting the ray at Z. (iv) Join X to Z. (v) Bisect each side and join each vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side to draw the three medians, which meet at a single point (the centroid). Hence they are concurrent.

questions.question: Construct the ΔKLM in which m KL = 4.8 cm, m LM = 5.2 cm and m MK = 4.5 cm; draw its altitudes and verify their concurrency.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw LM = 5.2 cm. (ii) With L as centre radius 4.8 cm and with M as centre radius 4.5 cm, draw arcs intersecting at K. (iii) Join K to L and K to M. (iv) Draw the perpendiculars from K to LM, from L to MK and from M to KL. All three altitudes pass through a single common point O, verifying their concurrency (O is the orthocentre).

questions.question: Construct the ΔPQR in which m PQ = 7 cm, m QR = 6.5 cm and m PR = 5.8 cm; find its perpendicular bisectors and verify their concurrency.
questions.answer: The three perpendicular bisectors are concurrent (circumcentre).
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw QR = 6.5 cm. (ii) With Q as centre radius 7 cm and with R as centre radius 5.8 cm, draw arcs intersecting at P. (iii) Join P to Q and P to R. (iv) Construct the perpendicular bisectors of PQ, QR and RP. All three pass through a single common point O, verifying their concurrency (O is the circumcentre).

questions.question: Construct a rectangle whose adjacent sides are 2.5 cm and 5 cm respectively. Construct a square having area equal to the given rectangle.
questions.explanation: The area of the rectangle = 2.5 × 5 = 12.5 cm<sup>2</sup>. The required square has area 12.5 cm<sup>2</sup>, so its side = √12.5 ≈ 3.54 cm. Construction: (i) Draw rectangle ABCD with AB = 5 cm, BC = 2.5 cm. (ii) Produce AB and on it mark AE = BC (so that the rectangle on AB with side BC becomes a square of side AB+...). Standard method: Produce AB to E such that BE = BC; bisect AE at M; draw a semicircle on AE; produce BC to meet the semicircle at F; then BF is the side of the required square. Construct the square on BF.

questions.question: Construct a square equal in area to a rectangle whose adjacent sides are 4.5 cm and 2.2 cm respectively. Measure the side of the square and find its area; compare with the area of the rectangle. Also verify that the perimeter of the square is less than that of the rectangle.
questions.answer: Square side ≈ 3.15 cm; area ≈ 9.9 cm<sup>2</sup>; perimeter of square < perimeter of rectangle.
questions.explanation: Area of rectangle = 4.5 × 2.2 = 9.9 cm<sup>2</sup>. The square of equal area has side = √9.9 ≈ 3.15 cm, so its area ≈ 9.9 cm<sup>2</sup>, which equals the rectangle's area. Perimeter of square = 4 × 3.15 ≈ 12.6 cm; perimeter of rectangle = 2(4.5 + 2.2) = 13.4 cm. Hence the perimeter of the square (12.6 cm) is less than that of the rectangle (13.4 cm).

questions.question: Construct a triangle having base 4 cm and the other two sides equal to 3.6 cm and 3.8 cm each. Transform it into a rectangle with equal area.
questions.answer: The rectangle has area equal to that of the triangle (base × ½ height).
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw AB = 4 cm. (ii) With A as centre radius 3.6 cm and with B as centre radius 3.8 cm, draw arcs meeting at C; join C to A and B. (iii) Draw CD ⊥ AB (the height h). The area of the triangle is ½ × 4 × h. (iv) Construct a rectangle on base AD (or on a convenient side) and of the same height half... standard method: construct a rectangle whose base equals the half of AB and whose height equals CD, so that its area = ½ × AB × CD = area of the triangle. Hence the required rectangle has equal area to the triangle.

questions.question: Construct a triangle having base 6 cm and the other two sides equal to 5 cm and 6 cm each. Construct a rectangle equal in area to the given triangle.
questions.answer: The rectangle has the same area as the triangle.
questions.explanation: Steps: (i) Draw AB = 6 cm. (ii) With A as centre radius 5 cm and with B as centre radius 6 cm, draw arcs meeting at C; join C to A and B. (iii) Draw CD ⊥ AB (height h). Area of the triangle = ½ × AB × h = ½ × 6 × h = 3h cm<sup>2</sup>. (iv) Construct a rectangle with base 3 cm and height h; its area = 3 × h = area of the triangle. Hence the required rectangle has area equal to that of ΔABC.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The side of a right triangle opposite to the right angle is ________.
questions.explanation: The side opposite the right angle in a right triangle is called the hypotenuse.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The line segment joining a vertex of a triangle and perpendicular to its opposite side is called an ________.
questions.explanation: A segment from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side is an altitude of the triangle.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: A line segment drawn from a vertex of a triangle and meeting the mid-point of its opposite side is called a ________.
questions.explanation: A segment from a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side is a median.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are ________.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent (they meet at the circumcentre).

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Two or more than two triangles are said to be congruent if they are equiangular and the measures of their corresponding sides are ________.
questions.explanation: Congruent triangles are equiangular with equal (corresponding) sides.

questions.question: A triangle having all three sides congruent is called a ________ triangle.
questions.explanation: A triangle with all three sides equal is an equilateral triangle.
questions.optionsRaw: a) scalene  b) right angled  c) equilateral  d) isosceles

questions.question: A quadrilateral having each angle equal to 90° and all sides congruent is called a ________.
questions.explanation: A quadrilateral with four right angles and four equal sides is a square.
questions.optionsRaw: a) parallelogram  b) rectangle  c) trapezium  d) square

questions.question: The medians of a triangle are ________.
questions.explanation: The three medians of a triangle are concurrent (they meet at the centroid).
questions.optionsRaw: a) collinear  b) congruent  c) concurrent  d) parallel

questions.question: The ________ altitudes of an equilateral triangle are congruent.
questions.explanation: In an equilateral triangle all three altitudes are equal in length.
questions.optionsRaw: a) two  b) three  c) four  d) none

questions.question: The diagonals of a rectangle ________ each other.
questions.explanation: The diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other (they are also equal, but they do not meet at right angles unless it is a square).
questions.optionsRaw: a) bisect  b) trisect  c) bisect at right angle  d) none of these

questions.question: The ________ of a triangle cut each other in the ratio 2 : 1.
questions.explanation: The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1, so it is the medians that cut each other in the ratio 2 : 1.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Altitudes  b) Angle bisectors  c) Right bisectors  d) Medians

questions.question: If each angle on the base of an isosceles triangle is 45°, then the measure of the third angle is ________.
questions.explanation: The two base angles are each 45°, so the third angle = 180° − (45° + 45°) = 90°.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 30°  b) 60°  c) 90°  d) 120°

questions.question: If the three medians of a triangle are congruent, then the triangle is ________.
questions.explanation: If all three medians are equal, the triangle is equilateral.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Right angled  b) equilateral  c) Isosceles  d) acute angled

questions.question: If two ________ of a triangle are congruent, then the triangle will be isosceles.
questions.explanation: If two sides of a triangle are congruent, then by definition the triangle is isosceles.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Altitudes  b) Medians  c) Right bisectors  d) sides

questions.question: In the given figure ABCD is a parallelogram and EFCD is a rectangle, also AL ⊥ DC. Prove that (i) ■ABCD = ■EFCD, (ii) ■ABCD = mDC × mAL.
questions.explanation: Proof (i): ABCD is a parallelogram and EFCD is a rectangle on the same base DC and between the same parallels DC and AF (since AE and DF are parallel to the base DC). By Theorem 14.1.1, parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallel lines are equal in area, so ■ABCD = ■EFCD. Q.E.D.  Proof (ii): ■EFCD is a rectangle, so its area = length × breadth = mDC × mED. Since AL ⊥ DC and ED ⊥ DC, AL and ED are each the perpendicular distance between the parallels DC and AF, hence mED = mAL. Therefore ■ABCD = ■EFCD = mDC × mAL. Q.E.D.

questions.question: In the given figure, if the diagonals of a quadrilateral separate it into four triangles of equal area, show that it is a parallelogram.
questions.answer: The quadrilateral ABCD is a parallelogram.
questions.explanation: Proof: Let the diagonals AC and BD of quadrilateral ABCD meet at O and let ■AOB = ■BOC = ■COD = ■DOA (all equal in area). Consider ■ABC: the median BO (O is the midpoint of AC because BO divides ■ABC into two equal triangles AOB and BOC) meets AC at O. Similarly, from ■BOC and ■COD equal in area, O is the midpoint of BD. Since the diagonals AC and BD bisect each other at O, the quadrilateral ABCD is a parallelogram. Q.E.D.

questions.question: In the given figure BC ∥ AD. ABC is a right-angled triangle at vertex B with mBC = 7 cm and mAC = 11 cm; also ΔABC and ΔBCD are on the same base BC. Find the area of ΔBCD.
questions.explanation: Since ΔABC is right-angled at B, mAB = √(mAC<sup>2</sup> − mBC<sup>2</sup>) = √(11<sup>2</sup> − 7<sup>2</sup>) = √(121 − 49) = √72 = 6√2 cm. So area of ΔABC = ½ × mBC × mAB = ½ × 7 × 6√2 = 21√2 cm<sup>2</sup>. Because BC ∥ AD, the triangles ABC and BCD stand on the same base BC and between the same parallel lines, so by Theorem 14.1.3 they are equal in area. Hence area of ΔBCD = 21√2 cm<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Show that a median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of equal area.
questions.answer: A median divides the triangle into two triangles of equal area.
questions.explanation: Proof: In ΔABC let AD be the median to BC, so D is the midpoint of BC, i.e. mBD = mDC. Drop the perpendicular (altitude) from A to BC; let its length be h. Then area of ΔABD = ½ × mBD × h and area of ΔADC = ½ × mDC × h. Since mBD = mDC, the two areas are equal. Hence ▲ABD = ▲ADC. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Show that the line segment joining the mid-points of the opposite sides of a rectangle divides it into two equal rectangles.
questions.answer: The two resulting rectangles are equal in area.
questions.explanation: Proof: Let ABCD be a rectangle and let E and F be the mid-points of the opposite sides AD and BC respectively. The segment EF is perpendicular to AD and BC and is parallel to AB and DC. So ABFE and EFCD are both rectangles on equal bases mAE = mED (since E is the midpoint of AD) and having the same altitude mAB = mDC. By Theorem 14.1.2 (parallelograms on equal bases and of equal altitudes are equal in area), ■ABFE = ■EFCD. Hence the rectangle is divided into two equal rectangles. Q.E.D.

questions.question: If two parallelograms of equal areas have the same or equal bases, their altitudes are equal.
questions.answer: The altitudes of the two parallelograms are equal.
questions.explanation: Proof: Let ABCD and EFGH be two parallelograms with equal areas, ■ABCD = ■EFGH, on equal bases mBC = mFG, with altitudes h₁ and h₂ respectively. Area = base × altitude, so ■ABCD = mBC × h₁ and ■EFGH = mFG × h₂. Since the areas and the bases are equal, mBC × h₁ = mFG × h₂ gives h₁ = h₂. Hence the altitudes are equal. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Show that an angle bisector of an equilateral triangle divides it into two triangles of equal areas.
questions.answer: The angle bisector divides the equilateral triangle into two triangles of equal area.
questions.explanation: Proof: Let ABC be an equilateral triangle with mAB = mBC = mCA, and let the bisector of ∠A meet BC at D. In an equilateral triangle the angle bisector of a vertex is also the median to the opposite side, so D is the midpoint of BC, i.e. mBD = mDC. Using the common altitude from A to BC (length h), area of ΔABD = ½ × mBD × h = ½ × mDC × h = area of ΔADC. Hence ▲ABD = ▲ADC, i.e. the two triangles have equal areas. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that a rhombus is divided by its diagonals into four triangles of equal areas.
questions.answer: Each of the four triangles has equal area.
questions.explanation: Proof: Let the diagonals of rhombus ABCD meet at O. The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so O is the midpoint of both AC and BD. Consider ΔABC: BO is a median (O is the midpoint of AC), so it divides ΔABC into two equal-area triangles ▲AOB = ▲BOC. Similarly in ΔBCD, CO is a median (O is the midpoint of BD), so ▲BOC = ▲COD, and likewise ▲COD = ▲DOA. Thus ▲AOB = ▲BOC = ▲COD = ▲DOA; the rhombus is divided by its diagonals into four triangles of equal area. Q.E.D.

questions.question: True or False: Area of a closed figure means the region enclosed by the bounding lines of the figure.
questions.explanation: By definition the area of a closed figure is the measure of the region enclosed by its boundary (bounding) lines.

questions.question: True or False: A diagonal of a rectangle divides it into two congruent triangles.
questions.explanation: A diagonal of a rectangle divides it into two right-angled triangles that are congruent (S.A.S.), since opposite sides are equal and each angle is 90°.

questions.question: True or False: Congruent figures have different areas.
questions.explanation: Congruent figures are exactly alike in shape and size, so they always have equal areas, not different areas.

questions.question: True or False: The area of a parallelogram is equal to the product of base and height.
questions.explanation: The area of a parallelogram equals base × perpendicular height (its altitude).

questions.question: True or False: Median of a triangle means the perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side (base).
questions.explanation: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side is the altitude, not the median.

questions.question: True or False: Perpendicular distance between two parallel lines can sometimes be different.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular distance between two parallel lines is the same (constant) everywhere along them.

questions.question: True or False: An altitude drawn from a vertex always bisects the opposite side.
questions.explanation: An altitude is perpendicular to the opposite side but does not necessarily bisect it. (It bisects the opposite side only in special triangles such as isosceles or equilateral.)

questions.question: True or False: Two triangles are equal in area, if they have the same base and equal altitude.
questions.explanation: By Theorem 14.1.3 / 14.1.4, triangles on the same (or equal) bases and of equal altitudes are equal in area.

questions.question: If the perpendicular distance between two lines is the same, the lines are ________.
questions.explanation: Two lines whose perpendicular distance is the same (constant) everywhere are parallel to each other.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Perpendicular to each other  b) Parallel to each other  c) Intersecting to each other  d) None of these

questions.question: If two triangles have equal areas then they will ________ be congruent as well.
questions.explanation: Equal areas do not force equal shapes. Two triangles of equal area need not be congruent (e.g. a tall thin triangle and a short wide triangle can have the same area). Hence they are "not necessarily" congruent. (Note: the printed key gives "Necessarily", which is mathematically incorrect.)
questions.optionsRaw: a) Not necessarily  b) Necessarily  c) Definitely  d) None of these

questions.question: Perpendicular from a vertex of a triangle to its opposite side is called ________.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular drawn from a vertex of a triangle to its opposite side (the base) is called the altitude of the triangle.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Median  b) Perpendicular bisector  c) Altitude  d) Angle bisector

questions.question: Parallelograms having the same base and the same altitude are ________.
questions.explanation: By Theorem 14.1.1 / 14.1.2, parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels (of the same altitude) are equal in area. They need not be congruent or similar, so the correct answer is "equal in areas". (Note: the printed key gives "All of these", which is mathematically incorrect.)
questions.optionsRaw: a) Congruent  b) Equal in areas  c) Similar  d) All of these

questions.question: Two parallelograms have equal bases. They will have the same area, if ________.
questions.explanation: All three conditions describe the same requirement: equal bases and equal altitudes (i.e. lying between the same parallel lines) give equal areas by Theorem 14.1.2. So all of these are correct.

options.text: They lie between the same parallel lines

questions.optionsRaw: a) Their altitudes are equal  b) Their altitude is the same  c) They lie between the same parallel lines  d) All of these

questions.question: ΔABC and ΔDEF have equal bases and equal altitudes, then the triangles are ________.
questions.explanation: By Theorem 14.1.4, triangles on equal bases and of equal altitudes are equal in area. Equal bases and altitudes do not make them congruent or similar. (Note: the printed key gives "Congruent", which is mathematically incorrect.)
questions.optionsRaw: a) Equal in area  b) Congruent  c) Similar  d) None of these

chapters.title: Projection of a side of a Triangle

questions.question: Find the length of AB and the area of ΔABC when mAC = 3 cm, mBC = 6 cm and m∠C = 120°.
questions.explanation: The obtuse angle is at C. By the law of cosines on ΔABC, AB<sup>2</sup> = AC<sup>2</sup> + BC<sup>2</sup> − 2·AC·BC·cos C = 3<sup>2</sup> + 6<sup>2</sup> − 2·3·6·cos120° = 9 + 36 − 36·(−½) = 45 + 18 = 63. So mAB = √63 = 3√7 cm. Area = ½·AC·BC·sin C = ½·3·6·sin120° = 9·(√3/2) = 9√3/2 cm<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Find the length of AB and the area of ΔABC when mAC = 40 mm, mBC = 80 mm and m∠C = 120°.
questions.explanation: Convert to cm: AC = 4 cm, BC = 8 cm; the obtuse angle is at C. By the law of cosines, AB<sup>2</sup> = AC<sup>2</sup> + BC<sup>2</sup> − 2·AC·BC·cos C = 4<sup>2</sup> + 8<sup>2</sup> − 2·4·8·cos120° = 16 + 64 + 32 = 112. So mAB = √112 = 4√7 cm. Area = ½·4·8·sin120° = 16·(√3/2) = 8√3 cm<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Find the length of AC in ΔABC when mBC = 6 cm, mAB = 4√2 cm and m∠ABC = 135°. If possible find the area of ΔABC.
questions.explanation: The side opposite ∠B is AC. By the law of cosines, AC<sup>2</sup> = AB<sup>2</sup> + BC<sup>2</sup> − 2·AB·BC·cos B = (4√2)<sup>2</sup> + 6<sup>2</sup> − 2·4√2·6·cos135° = 32 + 36 − 48√2·(−√2/2) = 68 + 48 = 116. So mAC = √116 cm. Area = ½·AB·BC·sin B = ½·4√2·6·sin135° = 12√2·(√2/2) = 12 cm<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Find the length of AC in ΔABC when mBC = 6√2 cm, mAB = 8 cm and m∠ABC = 135°. If possible find the area of ΔABC.
questions.explanation: The side opposite ∠B is AC. By the law of cosines, AC<sup>2</sup> = AB<sup>2</sup> + BC<sup>2</sup> − 2·AB·BC·cos B = 8<sup>2</sup> + (6√2)<sup>2</sup> − 2·8·6√2·cos135° = 64 + 72 − 96√2·(−√2/2) = 136 + 96 = 232. So mAC = √232 cm. Area = ½·AB·BC·sin B = ½·8·6√2·sin135° = 24√2·(√2/2) = 24 cm<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: In ΔABC, m∠A = 30°, prove that (mBC)<sup>2</sup> = (mAC)<sup>2</sup> + (mAB)<sup>2</sup> − √3(mAB)(mAC).
questions.explanation: Proof: ∠A is acute, so by Theorem 15.1.2, BC<sup>2</sup> = AC<sup>2</sup> + AB<sup>2</sup> − 2(AB)(projection of AC on AB). The projection of AC on AB is AD = AC·cos A = AC·cos30° = AC·(√3/2). Hence BC<sup>2</sup> = AC<sup>2</sup> + AB<sup>2</sup> − 2(AB)(AC)(√3/2) = AC<sup>2</sup> + AB<sup>2</sup> − √3(AB)(AC). Q.E.D.

questions.question: In ΔABC, calculate mBC when mAB = 6 cm, mAC = 5 cm and m∠A = 60°.
questions.explanation: By the law of cosines, BC<sup>2</sup> = AB<sup>2</sup> + AC<sup>2</sup> − 2·AB·AC·cos A = 6<sup>2</sup> + 5<sup>2</sup> − 2·6·5·cos60° = 36 + 25 − 60·(½) = 61 − 30 = 31. Hence mBC = √31 cm ≈ 5.57 cm.

questions.question: Whether the triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm is acute, obtuse or right-angled?
questions.explanation: Check the largest side: 5<sup>2</sup> = 25 and 3<sup>2</sup> + 4<sup>2</sup> = 9 + 16 = 25. Since the square of the largest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is right-angled (converse of Pythagoras theorem).

questions.question: Find the length of the median of side BC of ΔABC where mAB = 4 cm, mAC = 3 cm and mBC = 6 cm.
questions.explanation: Let AD be the median to BC, so D is the midpoint of BC and mBD = mCD = 3 cm. By Apollonius' theorem, AB<sup>2</sup> + AC<sup>2</sup> = 2(BD)<sup>2</sup> + 2(AD)<sup>2</sup>. So 4<sup>2</sup> + 3<sup>2</sup> = 2(3)<sup>2</sup> + 2(AD)<sup>2</sup>, i.e. 16 + 9 = 18 + 2(AD)<sup>2</sup>, giving 2(AD)<sup>2</sup> = 7 and AD = √(7/2) = √14/2 cm ≈ 1.87 cm.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In a right-angled ΔABC, (mAB)<sup>2</sup> + ________ = (mAC)<sup>2</sup>.
questions.explanation: In a right-angled triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. Here AC is the hypotenuse, so (mAB)<sup>2</sup> + (mBC)<sup>2</sup> = (mAC)<sup>2</sup>; the blank is (mBC)<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In ΔABC, two sides are equal to 4 cm; it is called ________ triangle.
questions.explanation: A triangle with two equal sides is called an isosceles triangle.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In ΔABC with m∠B = 90°, then (mAB)<sup>2</sup> + (mBC)<sup>2</sup> = ________.
questions.explanation: With the right angle at B, AC is the hypotenuse, so by Pythagoras' theorem (mAB)<sup>2</sup> + (mBC)<sup>2</sup> = (mAC)<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 8 cm, 15 cm and 17 cm are the sides of a ________.
questions.explanation: Check the largest side: 17<sup>2</sup> = 289 and 8<sup>2</sup> + 15<sup>2</sup> = 64 + 225 = 289. Since the square of the largest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is right-angled.

questions.question: In ΔABC, mAC = 3 cm, mBC = 6 cm and m∠C = 120°. Compute mAB.
questions.explanation: The obtuse angle is at C. By the law of cosines, AB<sup>2</sup> = AC<sup>2</sup> + BC<sup>2</sup> − 2·AC·BC·cos C = 3<sup>2</sup> + 6<sup>2</sup> − 2·3·6·cos120° = 9 + 36 + 18 = 63. Hence mAB = √63 = 3√7 cm ≈ 7.94 cm.

questions.question: Using the distance formula find the distance between the points (−4, 5) and (6, 6).
questions.explanation: d = √[(6 − (−4))<sup>2</sup> + (6 − 5)<sup>2</sup>] = √(10<sup>2</sup> + 1<sup>2</sup>) = √(100 + 1) = √101 units.

questions.question: Using the distance formula find the distance between the points (2, 2) and (2, 3).
questions.explanation: d = √[(2 − 2)<sup>2</sup> + (3 − 2)<sup>2</sup>] = √(0 + 1) = 1 unit.

questions.question: Using the distance formula find the distance between the points (0, 1) and (2, 3).
questions.explanation: d = √[(2 − 0)<sup>2</sup> + (3 − 1)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4 + 4) = √8 = 2√2 units.

questions.question: Using the distance formula find the distance between the points (0, 1) and (2, 3).
questions.explanation: d = √[(2 − 0)<sup>2</sup> + (3 − 1)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4 + 4) = √8 = 2√2 units. (This pair is the same as part (iii) in the book.)

questions.question: A(a, 0) and B(0, b) are points on the axes; find the distance AB when a = −3, b = −4.
questions.explanation: The distance from origin is AB = √(a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup>) = √((−3)<sup>2</sup> + (−4)<sup>2</sup>) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 units.

questions.question: A(a, 0) and B(0, b) are points on the axes; find the distance AB when a = −9, b = 6.
questions.explanation: AB = √(a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup>) = √((−9)<sup>2</sup> + 6<sup>2</sup>) = √(81 + 36) = √117 units.

questions.question: A(a, 0) and B(0, b) are points on the axes; find the distance AB when a = 3, b = 4.
questions.explanation: AB = √(a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup>) = √(3<sup>2</sup> + 4<sup>2</sup>) = √(9 + 16) = 5 units.

questions.question: A(a, 0) and B(0, b) are points on the axes; find the distance AB when a = √2, b = −2√2.
questions.explanation: AB = √(a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup>) = √((√2)<sup>2</sup> + (−2√2)<sup>2</sup>) = √(2 + 8) = √10 units.

questions.question: Find the perimeter of the triangle formed by the points A(0, 0), B(4, 0) and C(2, 2√3).
questions.explanation: AB = √[(4 − 0)<sup>2</sup> + 0<sup>2</sup>] = 4 units. BC = √[(2 − 4)<sup>2</sup> + (2√3 − 0)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4 + 12) = 4 units. CA = √[(0 − 2)<sup>2</sup> + (0 − 2√3)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4 + 12) = 4 units. Since all three sides are 4 units, the triangle is equilateral and its perimeter = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 units.

questions.question: Show that the points P(−3, −4), Q(2, 6) and R(0, 2) are collinear.
questions.answer: The points P, Q and R are collinear.
questions.explanation: PQ = √[(2+3)<sup>2</sup> + (6+4)<sup>2</sup>] = √(25 + 100) = √125 = 5√5. QR = √[(0−2)<sup>2</sup> + (2−6)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4 + 16) = √20 = 2√5. PR = √[(0+3)<sup>2</sup> + (2+4)<sup>2</sup>] = √(9 + 36) = √45 = 3√5. Now QR + PR = 2√5 + 3√5 = 5√5 = PQ. Since the sum of two distances equals the third, the points are collinear.

questions.question: Show that the points A(−1, 0), B(1, 0) and C(0, √3) are not collinear.
questions.answer: The points A, B and C are not collinear.
questions.explanation: AB = √[(1+1)<sup>2</sup> + 0] = 2. BC = √[(0−1)<sup>2</sup> + (√3−0)<sup>2</sup>] = √(1 + 3) = 2. CA = √[(−1−0)<sup>2</sup> + (0−√3)<sup>2</sup>] = √(1 + 3) = 2. All three sides equal 2, so no two distances add up to the third (instead they form an equilateral triangle). Hence the points are not collinear.

questions.question: Show that L(0, √3), M(−1, 0) and N(1, 0) form an equilateral triangle.
questions.explanation: LM = √[(−1−0)<sup>2</sup> + (0−√3)<sup>2</sup>] = √(1 + 3) = 2. MN = √[(1+1)<sup>2</sup> + 0] = 2. NL = √[(0−1)<sup>2</sup> + (√3−0)<sup>2</sup>] = √(1 + 3) = 2. Since LM = MN = NL = 2 units, the triangle is equilateral.

questions.question: Whether or not the points A(2, 3), B(8, 11) and C(0, 17) form an isosceles triangle.
questions.answer: Yes, ABC is an isosceles triangle.
questions.explanation: AB = √[(8−2)<sup>2</sup> + (11−3)<sup>2</sup>] = √(36 + 64) = 10. BC = √[(0−8)<sup>2</sup> + (17−11)<sup>2</sup>] = √(64 + 36) = 10. AC = √[(0−2)<sup>2</sup> + (17−3)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4 + 196) = √200 = 10√2. Since AB = BC = 10 units (two sides equal) and the points are non-collinear, ABC is an isosceles triangle.

questions.question: Do the points A(−1, 2), B(7, 5) and C(2, −6) form a right-angled triangle?
questions.answer: Yes, ABC is a right-angled triangle (right angle at A).
questions.explanation: AB = √[(7+1)<sup>2</sup> + (5−2)<sup>2</sup>] = √(64 + 9) = √73. AC = √[(2+1)<sup>2</sup> + (−6−2)<sup>2</sup>] = √(9 + 64) = √73. BC = √[(2−7)<sup>2</sup> + (−6−5)<sup>2</sup>] = √(25 + 121) = √146. Now AB<sup>2</sup> + AC<sup>2</sup> = 73 + 73 = 146 = BC<sup>2</sup>. By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem the triangle is right-angled (at A).

questions.question: If the points A(3, 1), B(9, 1) and C(6, k) determine an equilateral triangle, find the values of k.
questions.explanation: AB = √[(9−3)<sup>2</sup> + 0] = 6. For an equilateral triangle AC = BC = 6. Now AC<sup>2</sup> = (6−3)<sup>2</sup> + (k−1)<sup>2</sup> = 9 + (k−1)<sup>2</sup> = 36, giving (k−1)<sup>2</sup> = 27, so k − 1 = ±3√3 and k = 1 ± 3√3.

questions.question: Show that the points P(1, 2), Q(3, 4) and R(0, −1) are the vertices of a scalene triangle.
questions.explanation: PQ = √[(3−1)<sup>2</sup> + (4−2)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4 + 4) = 2√2. QR = √[(0−3)<sup>2</sup> + (−1−4)<sup>2</sup>] = √(9 + 25) = √34. RP = √[(1−0)<sup>2</sup> + (2+1)<sup>2</sup>] = √(1 + 9) = √10. Since PQ, QR and RP are all different in length and no one equals the sum of the other two, the points form a scalene (non-equilateral, non-isosceles, non-collinear) triangle.

questions.question: Show that the points A(2, 3), B(8, 11), C(0, 17) and D(−6, 9) are the vertices of a square.
questions.explanation: AB = √[(8−2)<sup>2</sup>+(11−3)<sup>2</sup>] = √(36+64) = 10. BC = √[(0−8)<sup>2</sup>+(17−11)<sup>2</sup>] = √(64+36) = 10. CD = √[(−6−0)<sup>2</sup>+(9−17)<sup>2</sup>] = √(36+64) = 10. DA = √[(2+6)<sup>2</sup>+(3−9)<sup>2</sup>] = √(64+36) = 10. So all four sides are equal. Diagonals: AC = √[(0−2)<sup>2</sup>+(17−3)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4+196) = √200 = 10√2 and BD = √[(−6−8)<sup>2</sup>+(9−11)<sup>2</sup>] = √(196+4) = √200 = 10√2. The diagonals are equal. Since all sides are equal and the diagonals are equal, ABCD is a square.

questions.question: Explain why the points A(−2, 0), B(0, −3), C(2, 0) and D(0, 3) determine a square?
questions.answer: All four sides are equal, so the figure determined is a rhombus (the printed key calls it a square).
questions.explanation: AB = √[(0+2)<sup>2</sup>+(−3−0)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4+9) = √13. BC = √[(2−0)<sup>2</sup>+(0+3)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4+9) = √13. CD = √[(0−2)<sup>2</sup>+(3−0)<sup>2</sup>] = √13. DA = √[(−2−0)<sup>2</sup>+(0−3)<sup>2</sup>] = √13. All four sides are equal (each √13). However the diagonals are AC = 4 and BD = 6, which are unequal. Hence the quadrilateral is a rhombus; it would be a square only if the diagonals were equal. (The printed key states "square".)

questions.question: Show that the points A(3, 2), B(4, 1), C(5, 4) and D(6, 3) are the vertices of a rectangle.
questions.explanation: AB = √[(4−3)<sup>2</sup>+(1−2)<sup>2</sup>] = √(1+1) = √2. BC = √[(5−4)<sup>2</sup>+(4−1)<sup>2</sup>] = √(1+9) = √10. CD = √[(6−5)<sup>2</sup>+(3−4)<sup>2</sup>] = √2. DA = √[(3−6)<sup>2</sup>+(2−3)<sup>2</sup>] = √10. So opposite sides are equal (AB = CD and BC = DA). Diagonals: AC = √[(5−3)<sup>2</sup>+(4−2)<sup>2</sup>] = √8 and BD = √[(6−4)<sup>2</sup>+(3−1)<sup>2</sup>] = √8, i.e. the diagonals are equal. Hence ABCD is a rectangle.

questions.question: Use the distance formula to show that the points O(0, 0), A(3, 0), B(5, 2) and C(2, 2) form the vertices of a parallelogram.
questions.explanation: OA = 3. AB = √[(5−3)<sup>2</sup>+(2−0)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4+4) = 2√2. BC = √[(2−5)<sup>2</sup>+(2−2)<sup>2</sup>] = 3. CO = √[(0−2)<sup>2</sup>+(0−2)<sup>2</sup>] = √(4+4) = 2√2. Hence OA = BC = 3 and AB = CO = 2√2, i.e. both pairs of opposite sides are equal. Therefore OABC is a parallelogram.

questions.question: Find the mid-point of the pair of points A(2, 6) and B(−4, 8) using the mid-point formula.
Find the mid-point of the pair of points P(−3, −1) and Q(5, 2) using the mid-point formula.
Find the mid-point of the pair of points L(0, 6) and M(−8, 0) using the mid-point formula.
Find the mid-point of the pair of points C(0, 0) and D(2√3, 4√3) using the mid-point formula.
questions.explanation: Mid-point = ((0+2√3)/2, (0+4√3)/2) = (√3, 2√3).

questions.question: Find the centre of a circle whose end points of a diameter are A(−5, 6) and B(3, −4).
questions.explanation: The centre of the circle is the mid-point of the diameter AB. Centre = ((−5+3)/2, (6+(−4))/2) = (−2/2, 2/2) = (−1, 1).

questions.question: The centre of a circle is (3, 4) and one end point of a diameter is (4, 6); find the other end point (B).
questions.explanation: Let the other end be B(x, y). The centre is the mid-point of the diameter, so (3, 4) = ((4+x)/2, (6+y)/2). Hence (4+x)/2 = 3 giving x = 2, and (6+y)/2 = 4 giving y = 2. So B = (2, 2).

questions.question: A circle has a diameter between the points A(−3, 4) and B(11, 6). Find the centre and radius of the circle.
questions.explanation: Centre = mid-point of AB = ((−3+11)/2, (4+6)/2) = (8/2, 10/2) = (4, 5). Radius = ½ AB = ½√[(11+3)<sup>2</sup>+(6−4)<sup>2</sup>] = ½√(196+4) = ½√200 = ½·10√2 = 5√2 units.

questions.question: Prove that a triangle is an isosceles triangle if and only if it has two equal medians.
questions.answer: The proof follows by the mid-point formula.
questions.explanation: Proof: Place the triangle with vertices A(0,0), B(a,0) and C(b,c). The mid-point of BC is ((a+b)/2, c/2), of AC is (b/2, c/2) and of AB is (a/2, 0). The median from A to BC has length m₀ = √[((a+b)/2)<sup>2</sup> + (c/2)<sup>2</sup>]; the median from B to AC has length √[((b−2a)/2)<sup>2</sup> + (c/2)<sup>2</sup>]. Setting these equal and simplifying leads precisely to the condition that two sides of the triangle are equal (AC = BC in this placement), i.e. the triangle is isosceles. Thus a triangle is isosceles if and only if two of its medians are equal. Q.E.D.

questions.question: Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
questions.answer: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
questions.explanation: Proof: Let A(0,0), B(a,0), D(b,c) and C(a+b, c) be the vertices of a parallelogram (AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC). The diagonal AC has mid-point ((a+b)/2, c/2). The diagonal BD has mid-point ((a+b)/2, c/2). Since both diagonals have the same mid-point, they bisect each other. Q.E.D.

questions.question: True or False: R is the mid-point of PQ if R is lying between P and Q.
questions.explanation: The mid-point R of segment PQ lies on the segment, i.e. between P and Q (at equal distances from P and Q). So a point lying between P and Q is the mid-point of PQ.

questions.question: True or False: In a scalene triangle all sides are equal.
questions.explanation: A scalene triangle has all three sides of different lengths. A triangle with all sides equal is equilateral.

questions.question: True or False: Perpendicular lines meet at an angle of 135°.
questions.explanation: Perpendicular lines meet at 90°, not 135°.

questions.question: True or False: Collinear points may form a triangle.
questions.explanation: Collinear points lie on a single straight line, so they cannot form a triangle.

questions.question: True or False: Non-collinear points form a triangle.
questions.explanation: Three non-collinear points determine a triangle.

questions.question: True or False: In an isosceles triangle, two base angles are equal.
questions.explanation: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides (the base angles) are equal.

questions.question: True or False: All the points that lie on the y-axis are collinear.
questions.explanation: Every point on the y-axis lies on the same single straight line (the y-axis), so they are collinear.

questions.question: True or False: The intersection of the x-axis and the y-axis is (0, 0).
questions.explanation: The x-axis and y-axis intersect at the origin, which is (0, 0).

questions.question: True or False: The distance from the origin to (6, 0) is 36 units.
questions.explanation: The distance from O(0,0) to (6,0) is √(6<sup>2</sup>+0<sup>2</sup>) = 6 units, not 36 units.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: If A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) are any two points, then |AB| = ________.
questions.explanation: This is the distance formula for the distance between two points.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Collinear points lie on the same ________.
questions.explanation: By definition, collinear points are points that lie on the same straight line.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In the 4th quadrant x > 0 and y ________.
questions.explanation: In the fourth quadrant the x-coordinate is positive and the y-coordinate is negative.

questions.question: Two perpendicular lines meet at an angle of:
questions.explanation: Perpendicular lines intersect at a right angle of 90°.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 45°  b) 60°  c) 90°  d) 180°

questions.question: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2) is called:
questions.explanation: The formula ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2) gives the mid-point of the segment joining two points, so it is the mid-point formula.
questions.optionsRaw: a) Mid-point formula  b) Distance formula  c) Division formula  d) Ratio formula

questions.question: A(3, 0) and B(0, 3) are two points in the plane; then |AB| =
questions.explanation: |AB| = √[(0−3)<sup>2</sup> + (3−0)<sup>2</sup>] = √(9 + 9) = √18 = 3√2 units.
questions.optionsRaw: a) 6 units  b) 6√2 units  c) 3√2 units  d) 3√2 units

questions.question: Three points A, B and C are collinear if:
questions.answer: (d) m AB + m BC = m AC
questions.explanation: For three collinear points, one of the three distances equals the sum of the other two. Here m AB + m BC = m AC means B lies between A and C, which is the condition for collinearity.

options.text: m AB = m BC + m AC
m AB + m BC = m AC

questions.optionsRaw: a) m AB = m BC + m AC  b) (m AB)<sup>2</sup> = (m BC)<sup>2</sup> + (m AC)<sup>2</sup>  c) both (a) and (b)  d) m AB + m BC = m AC
questions.correctAnswer: (d) m AB + m BC = m AC

questions.question: Identify 1/5 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: 1/5 is of the form p/q with integers p = 1, q = 5 (q ≠ 0), so it is rational. Its decimal form 0.2 is terminating.

questions.question: Identify √2 / 8 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: √2 is irrational; dividing an irrational number by the non-zero rational number 8 leaves it irrational.

questions.question: Identify 5/√6 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: √6 is irrational, so 5/√6 (a non-zero rational over an irrational) is irrational.

questions.question: Identify 2/8 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: 2/8 = 1/4 = 0.25, a terminating decimal, hence rational.

questions.question: Identify 1/√3 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: √3 is irrational; 1/√3 = √3/3 is also irrational.

questions.question: Identify √8 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: √8 = 2√2, and since √2 is irrational, √8 is irrational.

questions.question: Identify 0 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: 0 can be written as 0/1, i.e. p/q form, so it is rational.

questions.question: Identify π as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: π = 3.14159... is non-terminating and non-recurring, so it cannot be written as p/q; it is irrational.

questions.question: Identify √5 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: 5 is not a perfect square, so √5 = 2.236... is non-terminating non-recurring, hence irrational.

questions.question: Identify 22/3 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: 22/3 is a ratio of two integers, so it is rational (22/3 = 7.333... recurring).

questions.question: Identify 1/π as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: π is irrational, so 1/π is also irrational.

questions.question: Identify 11/12 as a rational or irrational number.
questions.explanation: 11/12 = 0.91666... is a recurring decimal formed by a ratio of integers, so it is rational.

questions.question: Convert 5/8 into a decimal fraction and state whether it is terminating or non-terminating.
questions.explanation: Divide 5 by 8: 8 × 0.625 = 5 exactly, so the decimal ends after three places.

questions.question: Convert 4/18 into a decimal fraction and state its type.
questions.explanation: 4/18 simplifies to 2/9. Long division gives 0.222..., the digit 2 repeats for ever.

questions.question: Convert 1/15 into a decimal fraction and state its type.
questions.explanation: 1/15 = 0.0 then 6 repeats, giving 0.0666...

questions.question: Convert 49/8 into a decimal fraction and state its type.
questions.explanation: 49 ÷ 8 = 6.125 exactly, so the decimal terminates.

questions.question: Convert 207/15 into a decimal fraction and state its type.
questions.explanation: 207 ÷ 15 = 13.8 exactly (15 × 13.8 = 207).

questions.question: Convert 50/76 into a decimal fraction and state its type.
questions.explanation: 50/76 reduces to 25/38. The remainder never becomes zero and the digits repeat, so it is non-terminating recurring.

questions.question: Illustrate 8/10 on the number line.
questions.answer: 8/10 = 0.8, marked 8 small divisions to the right of 0 on a scale divided into tenths (between 0 and 1).
questions.explanation: Divide each unit interval into 10 equal parts; 8/10 lies at the 8th mark after 0.

questions.question: Illustrate −8/10 on the number line.
questions.answer: −8/10 = −0.8, marked 8 small divisions to the left of 0 (between −1 and 0).
questions.explanation: The negative sign places the point on the left of the origin at the 8th tenth.

questions.question: Illustrate 1¼ on the number line.
questions.answer: 1¼ = 1.25, marked between 1 and 2, one quarter of the way from 1.
questions.explanation: After 1, divide the next unit into 4 parts and take the 1st mark.

questions.question: Illustrate −1¼ on the number line.
questions.answer: −1¼ = −1.25, marked between −2 and −1, one quarter of the way from −1 towards −2.
questions.explanation: Symmetric to 1¼ on the negative side.

questions.question: Illustrate 2/3 on the number line.
questions.answer: 2/3 ≈ 0.67, marked between 0 and 1, two thirds of the way from 0.
questions.explanation: Divide the interval 0-1 into 3 equal parts; 2/3 is at the 2nd mark.

questions.question: Illustrate −2/3 on the number line.
questions.answer: −2/3 ≈ −0.67, marked between −1 and 0, two thirds of the way from 0 to the left.
questions.explanation: Symmetric to 2/3 on the negative side.

questions.question: Can you make a list of all real numbers between 1 and 2?
questions.answer: No. The real numbers between 1 and 2 form an infinite set (indeed uncountable); no complete list can be made.
questions.explanation: Between any two distinct real numbers there are infinitely many more, so a finite listing is impossible.

questions.question: Give a reason why π (π) is an irrational number.
questions.answer: Because its decimal expansion is non-terminating and non-recurring, so it cannot be written in the form p/q.
questions.explanation: π = 3.14159265... never ends and never repeats a block of digits; every rational number has a terminating or recurring decimal, hence π is irrational.

questions.question: Tick the correct statement: 5/7 is an example of an irrational number.
questions.explanation: 5/7 is a ratio of integers, so it is rational.

questions.question: Tick the correct statement: π is an irrational number.
questions.explanation: π has a non-terminating non-recurring decimal expansion.

questions.question: Tick the correct statement: 0.31591... is an example of a non-terminating and non-recurring decimal fraction.
questions.explanation: The digits continue without ending and without a repeating pattern, which is the decimal signature of an irrational number.

questions.question: Tick the correct statement: 0.123 is an example of a recurring decimal fraction.
questions.explanation: 0.123 terminates, so it is not recurring.

questions.question: Tick the correct statement: 1/3 and 2/3 are lying between 0 and 1.
questions.explanation: 1/3 ≈ 0.33 and 2/3 ≈ 0.67, both greater than 0 and less than 1.

questions.question: Tick the correct statement: 1/√3 is an example of a rational number.
questions.explanation: √3 is irrational, so 1/√3 is irrational.

questions.question: Name the property: 1/2 + 2/3 = 2/3 + 1/2.
questions.explanation: Changing the order of the addends does not change the sum: a + b = b + a.

questions.question: Name the property: 4/3 + (1/3 + 2/3) = (4/3 + 1/3) + 2/3.
questions.explanation: The grouping of addends does not change the sum: a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c.

questions.question: Name the property: 9 × (10/9 + 20/9) = (9 × 10/9) + (9 × 20/9).
questions.answer: Left distributive property of multiplication over addition.
questions.explanation: a(b + c) = ab + ac: the 9 on the left multiplies each term inside the bracket.

questions.question: Name the property: (4/5 + 5/7) × 7/8 = (4/5 × 7/8) + (5/7 × 7/8).
questions.answer: Right distributive property of multiplication over addition.
questions.explanation: (b + c)a = ba + ca: the multiplier 7/8 is on the right.

questions.question: Name the property: (7/5 − 3/5) × 10/15 = (7/5 × 10/15) − (3/5 × 10/15).
questions.answer: Right distributive property of multiplication over subtraction.
questions.explanation: (b − c)a = ba − ca treats subtraction inside the bracket.

questions.question: Name the property: (d/c)(e/f) = (e/f)(d/c).
questions.explanation: The product is unchanged when the factors are interchanged: ab = ba.

questions.question: Name the property: 11 × (15 × 21) = (11 × 15) × 21.
questions.explanation: a(bc) = (ab)c: regrouping factors does not change the product.

questions.question: Name the property: (2/11) × (11/2) = (11/2) × (2/11) = 1.
questions.explanation: A number times its reciprocal equals 1: a × 1/a = 1.

questions.question: Name the property: (3/5) + (−3/5) = (−3/5) + (3/5) = 0.
questions.explanation: A number added to its negative gives the additive identity 0: a + (−a) = 0.

questions.question: Name the property: (a/b) × (b/a) = (b/a) × (a/b) = 1.
questions.explanation: The product of a number and its reciprocal is 1.

questions.question: Name the property: (15/10) × (8/5 − 4/10) = (15/10 × 8/5) − (15/10 × 4/10).
questions.answer: Left distributive property of multiplication over subtraction.
questions.explanation: a(b − c) = ab − ac.

questions.question: Name the property: (√2/3) × (3/√2) = (3/√2) × (√2/3) = 1.
questions.explanation: The two numbers are reciprocals, so their product is 1.
